id: My Kingdom for a Murmur of Fanfare

prompts.L1:

It’s common to live properly, to pretendyou don’t feel heat or grief: wave nightly at Miss Fugue and Mister Goggles before divinginto your nightcap, before reading yourself a bedtime story or watching your beloved sinkto the bottom of a lake and noting his absence in your log. The next day you drop his clothes offat Goodwill like a sack of mail from a warplane then hobble back to your hovel like a knight movingonly in Ls. It is comfortable to be alive this way, especially now, but it makes you so vulnerable to shock — you ignore the mortgage and find a falconer’s glove in your yard, whole hand still inside. Or you arrive homeafter a long day to discover your children have grown suddenly hideous and unlovable. What I’m tryingto say is I think it’s okay to accelerate around corners, to grunt back at the mailman and swallow allyour laundry quarters. So much of everything is dumb baffle: water puts out fire, my diseases can becomeyour diseases, and two hounds will fight over a feather because feathers are strange. All I want is to finallytake off my cowboy hat and show you my jeweled horns. If we slow dance I will ask you not to tugon them but secretly I will want that very much.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Miss, Fugue, Mister

outputs.L1:
It’s common to live properly, to pretend you don’t feel heat or grief: to wave nightly at Miss Fugue and Mister Goggles before diving into your nightcap, before reading yourself a bedtime story, or watching your beloved sink to the bottom of a lake and noting his absence in your log. The next day, you drop his clothes off at Goodwill like a sack of mail from a warplane, then hobble back to your hovel like a knight moving only in Ls.

It is comfortable to be alive this way, especially now, but it leaves you so vulnerable to shock—you ignore the mortgage and find a falconer’s glove in your yard, the whole hand still inside. Or you arrive home after a long day to discover that your children have grown suddenly hideous and unlovable.

What I’m trying to say is that I think it’s okay to accelerate around corners, to grunt back at the mailman, and to swallow all your laundry quarters. So much of everything is dumb baffle: water puts out fire, my diseases can become your diseases, and two hounds will fight over a feather because feathers are strange.

All I want is to finally take off my cowboy hat and show you my jeweled horns. If we slow-dance, I will ask you not to tug on them, but secretly, I will want that very much.
outputs.L2:
A respectable life often means acting as though sorrow and heat cannot touch you. Each evening, you bid Miss Fugue and Mister Goggles goodnight before slipping into your nightcap, telling yourself a bedtime tale, or observing your beloved descend to the floor of a lake and recording his disappearance in the log. In the morning, you deliver his clothing to Goodwill like wartime correspondence dropped from an aircraft, then limp toward your shack with the L-shaped progress of a chess knight.

Living like this is comfortable—particularly these days—but it leaves you dangerously open to surprise. You neglect the mortgage and discover a falconer’s glove on the lawn with the entire hand still lodged inside. Or, after an exhausting day, you return to find that your children have abruptly become repulsive and impossible to love.

What I mean is that perhaps there is nothing wrong with speeding through turns, answering the mailman with a growl, or gulping down every quarter meant for the washing machines. Much of existence is senseless obstruction: water extinguishes flame, my illnesses may turn into yours, and a pair of hounds will battle over a feather simply because feathers are peculiar.

More than anything, I want to remove my cowboy hat at last and reveal my gem-covered horns to you. If we dance slowly, I’ll tell you not to pull them, though privately I’ll be hoping very much that you do.
outputs.L3:
Living “properly” often requires people to suppress grief, ignore emotional pain, and continue performing their daily routines as though nothing has happened. Although this emotional detachment may provide a temporary sense of comfort and stability, it also leaves a person vulnerable to sudden, disturbing shocks when buried feelings or unexpected events break through the surface.

In response to this condition, the speaker suggests that unconventional, impulsive, or socially improper behavior may be a legitimate way of confronting life’s absurdity. Existence is often confusing and irrational, shaped by strange and unpredictable connections between people, events, and suffering. Conventional rules cannot always provide meaning or protection in such a world.

Ultimately, beneath the speaker’s defiance lies a desire for honesty and closeness. Rather than remaining hidden behind social expectations and emotional restraint, the speaker longs to reveal their true self and experience a vulnerable, intimate connection with another person.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the tension between emotional repression and the unpredictable absurdity of everyday life. Grief, fear, and loneliness do not appear in orderly or conventionally “poetic” forms; instead, they emerge through surreal images, awkward routines, and moments of dark comedy. This strange mixture of pain and humor reflects the mind’s attempt to continue functioning even when ordinary reality has become unsettling. Familiar habits offer the appearance of stability, yet they also reveal how easily routine can become a form of denial.

Throughout the poem, the speaker seems caught between concealing difficult feelings and allowing them to surface. Social expectations encourage composure, restraint, and normality, but the poem repeatedly disrupts those expectations with bizarre or uncomfortable details. Its absurd images therefore do more than create surprise: they expose the inadequacy of polite language and controlled behavior when faced with genuine emotional distress. Laughter becomes inseparable from sorrow, suggesting that dark humor can serve both as a defense against pain and as an honest response to life’s irrationality.

As the poem develops, it moves toward a rejection of emotional neatness. Rather than presenting vulnerability as weakness, it treats openness—even when messy, embarrassing, or strange—as a form of courage. The hidden self is not polished or easily explained, but revealing it makes authentic intimacy possible. By allowing grief, desire, confusion, and absurdity to coexist, the poem argues for a less guarded way of living.

Ultimately, the poem embraces unruly honesty over controlled appearances. It suggests that meaningful connection begins when people stop pretending to be entirely reasonable, stable, or untouched by suffering. To share one’s private strangeness is to risk exposure, but it is also to offer another person something genuine. In this way, the poem transforms vulnerability into an alternative to isolation: a difficult but liberating path toward fuller self-knowledge and deeper human connection.
outputs.L5:
**Miss Fugue and Mister Time**

Miss Fugue lived in a house of repeating hallways, where every door opened onto a memory she had nearly forgotten. Each morning, she played the piano, beginning with a single melody. Soon another voice followed, then another, weaving around the first until the room seemed full of invisible musicians.

Across the street lived Mister Time, who repaired clocks but never wore a watch.

“You are always returning to the beginning,” he told her.

“And you are always rushing toward the end,” Miss Fugue replied.

One evening, Mister Time crossed the street and sat beside her at the piano. She played the opening phrase. He answered with a second. Together, they let the music wander—forward, backward, and home again.

For once, Mister Time forgot the hour.

And Miss Fugue remembered everything.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about emotional repression, grief, domestic routine, and the secret desire to be seen, using dark humor and startling imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Every morning I butter the toast as if sealing a small, edible coffin.

The kettle screams. I admire its honesty.

In the cupboard, grief sits between the sugar and the paprika, wearing my mother’s old perfume and refusing to pay rent. I reach past it for the tea. We have an arrangement: I do not look directly at its many wet eyes, and it does not mention the hospital corridor, the unanswered phone, the winter coat still hanging in the hall with nobody inside it.

Domestic life continues, that famous little dictatorship.

I scrub the plates until their white faces forget us. I fold the towels into obedient rectangles. I vacuum around the shadow under the dining table, though the shadow has lately begun to breathe. At six, I chop an onion and blame it for everything.

“How was your day?” you ask.

“Fine,” I say, while a black horse kicks through my rib cage carrying telegrams from the dead.

We eat soup. The spoons perform their silver autopsies. Outside, the neighbors drag their bins to the curb, each one wheeling a plastic sarcophagus full of evidence. Someone laughs behind a fence. Somewhere a baby discovers it has been born and lodges an official complaint.

I have become excellent at not collapsing.

I can pay bills while full of ghosts. I can change the sheets with a mouthful of thunder. I can stand in the supermarket comparing detergents while my heart, dressed as a widow, throws itself into the freezer aisle.

Sometimes I leave a cabinet door open.

This is not forgetfulness. It is a flare.

Sometimes I sigh too loudly while washing a cup, hoping you will hear the cathedral cave in. Sometimes I pause in the doorway with my hands still wet, wanting you to turn and say, There you are. Not What’s wrong, not Did you buy milk, but There you are, as if I have been missing for years and have just staggered home from the forest with stars tangled in my hair.

Instead, the refrigerator hums its fluorescent hymn.

I close the cabinet.

I dry my hands.

Upstairs, grief is trying on my clothes again, admiring itself in the mirror, asking if this sorrow makes it look fat.

I tell it no.

I tell everyone no.

Then I set the table for three.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph contemporary prose poem that begins with “It’s common to live properly” and ends with an intimate confession involving jeweled horns.
counterfactuals.output: It’s common to live properly, to answer messages before the blue light fades, to buy pears in paper bags and call your mother from the train, while the city keeps refreshing its small catastrophes beneath your thumb. Still, dusk spills violet over the laundromat windows, and every shirt turns briefly into a flag for a country no one has survived. I come home carrying rain in my sleeves, your name warm behind my teeth, ready to admit what I have hidden through all our ordinary mornings: beneath my hair, I have been growing jeweled horns for you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an absurdist lyrical monologue in which a speaker argues that ordinary life is nonsensical, mixing mundane details like Goodwill, mortgages, laundry quarters, and the mailman with grotesque dream imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
You tell me life makes sense, and I ask: have you ever stood under the fluorescent judgment of Goodwill at 8:47 on a Tuesday, holding a soup ladle in one hand and a dead man’s bowling trophy in the other?

Exactly.

Everything is tagged, but nothing is priced correctly. Three dollars for a blouse. Ninety years for a body. A mortgage for a box with windows, where we lie awake listening to the pipes rehearse their small metallic apocalypse. Every month the bank sends a letter reminding us that the house belongs to a number wearing a necktie. We sign our names beneath it like obedient ghosts.

Meanwhile, the laundry demands quarters.

Not poetry. Not blood. Not a lock of hair from your first love. Quarters. Eight of them, bright as tiny moons, fed into the machine so your socks may tumble through the underworld. I have watched them revolve behind the glass, those shirts and towels, twisting together like pale animals caught in a flood. Once, I swear, the washer opened one blue eye and whispered, *You are also being cleaned for resale.*

And what could I say? I had no change left.

At night, the ceiling lowers itself by an inch. You don’t notice because you are calculating interest. But I notice. I see the chandelier grow teeth. I see the refrigerator kneel in the kitchen and give birth to a wet sack of hummingbirds. They crawl across the linoleum, each one wearing my mother’s face, each one asking why I never learned to fold a fitted sheet.

Ordinary life! You call it ordinary because terror has a schedule.

At nine, the mailman comes.

He walks up the path with his leather bag full of verdicts: coupons, condolences, credit-card offers, a catalog of patio furniture for the patio we do not own. He smiles as if he hasn’t just pushed a white envelope through the mouth of our house. I watch from behind the curtain. Sometimes his shadow arrives before he does and stands on the porch, removing its hat. Sometimes there is no mailman at all—only a tall heron in government shorts, pecking at the doorbell with a human finger.

Still, I say, “Thank you.”

That is the most grotesque part.

We thank the machinery. We thank the cashier. We thank the automated voice for keeping us on hold while our lives drip patiently into the carpet. We say “No worries” when there are clearly worries everywhere: nesting in the gutters, swelling under the floorboards, floating belly-up in the toilet tank.

At Goodwill, I once found a wedding veil beside a toaster. Tell me that isn’t theology. Tell me civilization is not merely a long receipt curling from the mouth of God.

We buy back our own discarded lamps. We insure our teeth. We put passwords on photographs of breakfast. We spend forty years paying for a roof and then climb onto it to clean leaves from a metal trench. Beneath us, the house chews quietly on our furniture.

And the dreams—don’t speak to me of dreams as if they are less real. Last night I was chased through a supermarket by a horse made of elbows. The aisles were stocked with jars of weather. Thunder was two for one. At the register, my father had become a centipede in a bathrobe, counting laundry quarters with all hundred hands.

“You’re short,” he said.

“I know,” I said, though I was the usual height.

Then the mailman burst from the freezer, covered in stamps, his tongue black with addresses. He handed me the mortgage. The mortgage was breathing. It had gills. It called me *Tenant* in the voice of a disappointed moon.

I woke to the alarm clock, which is a machine designed to make sure we never escape by sleeping.

So go on. Make coffee. Match the socks. Nod at the neighbors while their garage door rises like the jaw of a patient beast. Drive to work beneath a sky full of invisible teeth. Pretend the red light knows why it is red.

But do not tell me life makes sense.

Life is a receipt in a wet pocket. Life is a Goodwill mannequin dreaming of skin. Life is the mailman bringing a coupon for twenty percent off the coffin while the washing machine, stuffed with quarters, spins and spins and spins—

trying to remember which of us is the stain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly comic, dreamlike poem about someone coping with a beloved’s death by following daily routines, then gradually embracing strange and reckless impulses. Avoid line breaks and use long, flowing sentences.
counterfactuals.output: Every morning I make two cups of coffee, one for me and one for your absence, which takes its without sugar and leaves a black ring on the table like a tiny eclipse, then I water the plants, feed the cat, polish the teaspoons, and tell the toaster that we are coping beautifully, though it keeps coughing up burnt little telegrams from the underworld; at noon I fold your shirts into neat blue squares and stack them in the cupboard where they breathe softly through their buttons, and at night I brush my teeth for the recommended two minutes while your ghost sits on the washing machine, swinging its legs and criticizing my gums, but grief is a patient locksmith and soon the days begin opening doors I do not remember owning, so I wear your winter coat in July, eat birthday cake in the bath, mail our unpaid bills to the moon, and ride the last bus to the slaughterhouse just to ask the cows whether love has always been this badly managed; eventually I stop going to work and start attending the secret weddings of crows, I gamble our savings on a horse named Good Riddance, I climb the church steeple with pockets full of cutlery and rain spoons over the town, laughing as the citizens look up with their mouths open like hungry graves, and when the police ask me to come down carefully I tell them careful is how I lost you, careful is the clean shirt, the locked door, the pill taken with water, the obedient heart ticking in its little office, so I spread your coat like wings and step into the blue machinery of morning, not wanting to die exactly, only to surprise the world into giving you back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental prose poem in a surreal, emotionally vulnerable voice. Include a knight who moves only in Ls, a falconer’s glove with a hand inside, fighting hounds, a cowboy hat, and jeweled horns.
counterfactuals.output:
At night the knight moves only in Ls—  
left, then longing;  
love, then loss—  
never straight toward me.

I sleep beneath the chessboard  
where the black squares drip weather  
and the white squares whisper, *coward, coward,*  
though softly, as if afraid to wake my childhood.

In the kitchen, a falconer’s glove  
waits on the table  
with a hand inside.

Not severed.  
Not alive.  
Simply patient.

Outside, fighting hounds tear the moon  
into wet strips. Their growls enter the house  
wearing my mother’s perfume.  
I lock every door except the one in my chest,  
which has never understood doors.

You arrive in a cowboy hat,  
rain pooled in its brim,  
jeweled horns rising from your skull—  
rubies for rage, opals for the apologies  
you practiced but did not bring.

The knight turns another corner  
to avoid touching me.

I ask the glove what it remembers.  
The hand clenches once:

a bird,  
a wrist,  
the unbearable discipline of returning.

By morning the hounds are sleeping  
nose to bloodied nose.  
You hang your hat on one jeweled horn  
and kneel beside them.

I want to forgive you.

Instead, I move two rooms over  
and one room down,  
crooked as mercy,  
faithful as a wound  
to the strange rules that made it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
